summary: Weekly POC sync to review integration progress of Redwood SDK and tool/function calling for Aurora Health's patient-summary feature. Discussed streaming vs batch, structured output mapping, SDK error handling, and security requirements. Agreed on next perf runs and an infosec follow-up. Pricing and capacity options to be sent.
transcript:
[00:00] Liam Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. this is Liam from Redwood, joined by Priya our solutions engineer. um we are at 9:30 pacific. quick check, is timestamping okay?
[00:12] Maya Singh: Yep, all good here. thanks Liam.
[00:15] Liam Carter: Cool. quick agenda: 1) SDK integration status, 2) results from the pilot runs, 3) structured output mapping for the patient-summary microservice, 4) security ask. priya will cover the perf stuff.
[00:29] Priya Narang: Hi team. so we re-ran the 256 and 512 token runs yesterday with the quantized model as discussed. overall throughput improved ~1.6x on the 512 case when we enabled continuous batching, though peak latency at 99p moved from ~420ms to ~540ms under the same concurrency. there may be a mismatch in payload serialization causing extra overhead on your side.
[00:55] Daniel Ortiz: hmm we are still using the old http client at the moment, not the new async sdk. i can swap that this week. could the serialization be from the nested patient objects? we send a fairly deep json for context.
[01:12] Priya Narang: yeah that could be it, nested arrays cause larger payloads and we observed the python client serializes slower vs node. also the SDK has streaming on the wire which reduces perceived latency for the user facing flows.
[01:28] Ethan Park: just to add, for product we prefer earlier partial outputs for UX — streaming seems better — but cost is also a factor.
[01:37] Liam Carter: right — tradeoff. streaming reduces time-to-first-token but increases open connection time and can affect cost per session depending on your workload. we can show numbers in the sheet i'll share after.
[01:49] Maya Singh: for our compliance folks, we need to confirm that nothing is stored outside our logs, and encryption keys — we need KMS integration.
[01:58] Sofia Lee: yes, SOC 2 is table stakes. also audit logs and SSO for RBAC. do you support customer-managed keys on private?
[02:07] Liam Carter: on Redwood Private yes, customer-managed KMS/HSM is supported. for hosted we offer an encryption-at-rest model but for strict compliance Private or Dedicated with VPC peering is recommended.
[02:20] Sofia Lee: ok noted. can you send the exact spec in the compliance packet?
[02:25] Liam Carter: absolutely — i'll attach the compliance doc link.
[02:28] Priya Narang: back to perf — one anomaly: during the 512 run some requests fell back to a smaller variant model because of capacity constraints, which spiked latency. we suspect the auto fallback routing kicked in.
[02:42] Daniel Ortiz: interesting, we saw a couple of odd responses — some structured fields missing. could that be the variant change?
[02:48] Priya Narang: yes, that explains it. the smaller variant doesn't have the same structured-output wrapper and the sdk mapping didn't apply. for poc we can pin the model version to avoid that.
[03:00] Maya Singh: how easy is pinning? we need predictability for the clinical summarization.
[03:05] Priya Narang: it's a flag in the route configuration — we can lock to model v1.2-quant or provide a canary rollout where 95% traffic hits the main variant.
[03:14] Liam Carter: i'll propose two configs in the follow-up: pin vs canary. pricing varies.
[03:18] Ethan Park: on structured output — we want a stable JSON schema: patient.name, patient.diagnoses[], summary.sections[]. can the sdk enforce schema or validate?
[03:27] Priya Narang: currently the sdk returns the raw generated text or parsed function call output. for structured output we recommend function/tool calling where the model emits a json payload that maps to your contract. the sdk includes a lightweight validator helper that runs a jsonschema check client-side. it's not a server-side enforcement, though we can add server-side guardrails in redwood dedicated via response validators.
[03:48] Daniel Ortiz: can you show an example? we tried the function call with a simple schema but the model sometimes emits extra keys.
[03:55] Priya Narang: sure — example we sent in the deck earlier: 
  {
    "patient": {"name": "string", "id": "string"},
    "summary": [{"section": "string", "text": "string"}],
    "diagnoses": ["string"]
  }
we saw ~87% conformity in the last batch when using a combination of priming + function signatures. the remaining cases were minor key order differences or extra metadata keys.
[04:22] Maya Singh: 87% ok but we need higher for production, especially for downstream billing and alerts. what's the recommended path?
[04:29] Priya Narang: two levers: 1) stronger prompt engineering + stricter function schema, 2) a post-processor which runs a deterministic mapper and reconciliation rules. redwood optimize can suggest quantization and batching settings; we also provide a quality monitor to detect regression on the prompt set.
[04:49] Ethan Park: how would a post-processor handle hallucinated diagnosis strings? sometimes the model invents a less-likely entry.
[04:57] Priya Narang: the post-processor can cross-check against an authoritative code list (ICD-10) and flag unknown values, optionally backoff to a human-in-loop for ambiguous cases. we can wire that to a tool call to your internal lookup service.
[05:12] Daniel Ortiz: speaking of tools — we tried the tool calling flow to query our medication db via the sdk last week. link: https://redwood.company/poc/aurora/tool-logs (note: spoken in call). some errors came back as 502 when the payload exceeded 64KB. is that a redwood limit?
[05:29] Priya Narang: there's a payload size limit on the gateway — default 64kb for hosted; dedicated can be configured up to 256kb. recommended to keep payloads small and use a reference id pattern for large attachments.
[05:42] Maya Singh: we can change to reference ids, but that requires us to add a caching layer. do you have patterns?
[05:48] Priya Narang: yes — we've seen teams store the heavy ehr context in their own object store and send a short context pointer. redwood's kv cache pairs well with that for hot records to reduce fetch cost.
[06:00] Liam Carter: quick note: i'll share a patterns doc and a sample architecture diagram (link in notes).
[06:04] Sofia Lee: on network, if we go private, is there support for vpc peering and audit logs to our siem?
[06:11] Liam Carter: yes, vpc peering and syslog forwarding for audit logs are supported on private and dedicated. we'll include the exact syslog format in the compliance packet.
[06:21] Ethan Park: any blockers for this week? devs need clarity on sdk error semantics for retries. currently our retry logic retries idempotent requests only. we need guidance for streaming vs polling.
[06:32] Priya Narang: sdk exposes stable retry codes; for streaming we recommend exp backoff and cancel semantics. i'll put a small snippet in the follow-up. also note that function calls are idempotent if you include a client-provided idempotency key.
[06:46] Daniel Ortiz: good to know. for the perf runs, can you run a dedicated gpu case with 8 concurrency and 512 tokens? we'll test our app behavior with that pattern.
[06:56] Priya Narang: yes, that's in my list — i'll run that and share logs.
[07:01] Maya Singh: last thing — pricing. rough for committed capacity vs on-demand?
[07:07] Liam Carter: high level: hosted on-demand is per-token plus request overhead; dedicated is committed monthly with lower per-token and predictable latency. i'll include two scenarios in the sheet: 100k tokens/day hosted vs dedicated 1 gpu reserved.
[07:21] Ethan Park: perfect.
[07:24] Liam Carter: recap and next steps: i'll send the benchmark sheet + compliance packet, priya runs the dedicated perf, daniel uploads payload examples, sofia sends soc2 qs. then we schedule the infosec deep-dive next week. any other items?
[07:39] Maya Singh: nope that covers it. thanks.
[07:41] Liam Carter: thanks everyone. we'll share the links in the calendar invite and follow up.
[07:46] [meeting ends]
